common_name: White Christmas Cactus (Pure White Holiday Cactus)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; White Christmas needs the same fall regime of cool nights and long uninterrupted darkness as other Schlumbergera cultivars to set its pure white flower buds.

directions: Pot in a well-drained, humus-rich mix and place in bright indirect light, letting the top inch dry between waterings. White Christmas stands out among holiday cactus cultivars for flowers with almost no pink or cream blush, opening a clean, snowy white against the glossy green, scallop-edged stem segments typical of Schlumbergera truncata. Because it lacks the pigment that gives other cultivars their color, keep it out of intense sun, which can bleach or brown the delicate petals. Like its more colorful relatives, it needs roughly six weeks of cool nights and unbroken darkness in early fall to reliably set buds for the winter display.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Thor Christmas Cactus (Large-Flowered Orange-Red Holiday Cactus)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Thor's oversized blooms form heavily on vigorous, trailing growth, so give it a hanging basket or elevated pot and the standard fall cool-and-dark treatment to trigger flowering.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a well-drained, slightly acidic potting mix, watering thoroughly and then letting the surface dry before the next soak. Thor is prized among collectors for unusually large, vividly saturated orange-red flowers that dwarf those of older heirloom holiday cactus cultivars, set against robust, cascading stems well suited to a hanging basket. Its heavier bloom load draws more from the plant's reserves, so a dilute balanced fertilizer during the active growing season helps sustain the display. As with all Schlumbergera, six or more weeks of cool nights and uninterrupted darkness in autumn are needed to initiate the winter flower buds.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Madame Butterfly Christmas Cactus (Double-Flowered Cream Holiday Cactus)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Madame Butterfly's fully double blooms are heavier than single-flowered cultivars, so stake or support top-heavy stems and provide the usual fall dark treatment to set buds.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping it evenly moist while actively growing and slightly drier during its post-bloom rest. Madame Butterfly produces fully double, ruffled flowers in soft cream fading to blush pink, with extra layers of petals that give each bloom a fuller, rose-like shape than the single flat trumpets typical of the species. The extra petal count means flowers open more slowly and last longer on the plant than single-flowered cultivars, extending the holiday display by a week or more. Provide the same autumn regimen of cool nights and long unbroken darkness as other Schlumbergera cultivars to ensure a heavy bud set.

common_name: Caribbean Dancer Christmas Cactus (Bicolor Apricot-Pink Holiday Cactus)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Caribbean Dancer belongs to a bicolor breeding line prized for two-tone petals, and needs the standard fall cool-and-dark period to bloom well.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, letting the top of the mix dry slightly between waterings. Caribbean Dancer belongs to a group of bicolor Schlumbergera cultivars bred for petals shading from warm apricot-peach at the base to bright rose-pink at the tips, a two-tone effect unlike the solid-color flowers of older holiday cactus varieties. The layered coloring shows best in bright, indirect light, since low light can mute the contrast between the two tones. As with other Schlumbergera cultivars, roughly six weeks of cool nights and long uninterrupted darkness in fall are needed to set a full crop of winter flower buds.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Exotic Dancer Christmas Cactus (Bicolor Magenta-Purple Holiday Cactus)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Exotic Dancer is part of the same bicolor breeding line as Caribbean Dancer, and needs the standard fall cool-and-dark period to bloom well.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, watering thoroughly and then allowing the surface to dry before the next watering. Exotic Dancer is a sibling selection from the same bicolor Schlumbergera breeding line as Caribbean Dancer, but trades the apricot tones for a deeper, richer combination of magenta-pink shading into purple at the petal tips. The intense coloring makes it a standout among massed holiday cactus displays and shows best against a plain, uncluttered background. It shares the same autumn requirement for cool nights and long stretches of uninterrupted darkness to reliably initiate flower buds.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Rose Queen Easter Cactus (Deep Rose-Pink Spring Cactus)

planting.note: Root two- or three-segment stem cuttings after a brief callusing period in a well-drained, humus-rich orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light; Rose Queen needs the same autumn cool-and-dark rest as the species to reliably set its deep pink spring flower buds.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained mix amended with orchid bark, keeping the mix evenly moist through active growth and slightly drier during the post-bloom rest. Rose Queen is a long-cultivated Easter cactus selection valued for flowers in a deeper, more saturated rose-pink than the species' typical scarlet or salmon tones, opening in star-shaped clusters at the tips of the flattened, scalloped stem segments. Give it several weeks of cool nights and uninterrupted darkness in early autumn to set a full flush of spring buds, and avoid moving or rotating the plant once buds appear, since Hatiora often drops buds in response to disturbance. Keep it away from heating vents and cold drafts, which can also trigger bud drop.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Rose Easter Cactus (Dwarf Pink Spring Cactus)

planting.note: Root two- or three-segment stem cuttings after a brief callusing period in a well-drained, humus-rich orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light; this compact species needs the same autumn cool-and-dark rest as its larger relatives to set spring flower buds.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained mix amended with orchid bark, watering to keep the mix lightly moist during active growth and allowing it to dry a bit more during the cooler rest period. Hatiora rosea, formerly classified as Rhipsalidopsis rosea, is a smaller, more compact relative of the common Easter cactus, with slender, scalloped stem segments and profuse small, bright pink flowers that open in mid to late spring. Its dwarf, densely branching habit makes it well suited to small pots and shallow dish arrangements rather than the larger hanging baskets typical of Hatiora gaertneri. Because it is one of the wild parent species behind many modern Easter cactus hybrids, it shares the same need for a cool, dark autumn rest to trigger reliable spring flowering.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
